title: The Silent Killer in Tech: Why Burnout is a No Go
author: Colette Molteni
summary: Colette Molteni writes for tech professionals about spotting and heading off burnout through emotional intelligence and self-management. She uses three stories: a talented colleague whose unaddressed burnout turned into defensiveness and a written warning, a manager who shielded her team by calmly saying no to an unrealistic data request, and her own planned time off before a demanding month. Her main claim is that burnout is silent until someone, whether the individual, colleagues or managers, has the nerve to name it. For leaders, she argues that protecting a team means actually declining work and modelling rest rather than just talking about wellbeing. The piece is anecdotal and contains newsletter chrome, but the leadership lesson about boundaries and early recognition is clear.
points: Burnout can go unaddressed because colleagues excuse brilliant performers, as happened when a talented colleague's defensiveness escalated until it cost him a written warning.
The first step in diminishing burnout is acknowledging its presence rather than letting it stay silent.
A manager who calmly said no and offered a third of the requested metrics protected the team from burning out in a single day.
Leaders must live the practice of saying no and of taking planned breaks, because the team follows their example.
Rest scheduled in advance, with open communication with peers and boss, builds reserves before a high-pressure period.
quotes: We are human—not machines, not artificial intelligence, or some animate being that can withstand endless wear and tear.
But his manager, colleagues, and even him did not have the bravery to at least recognize it. Often, with burnout, the first step to diminishing it is acknowledging its presence.

She held the line, leveraging her skilled self-management ability to communicate a gentle No in a calm manner. She leveraged her high emotional intelligence to craft a response that still appeased the stakeholders by offering the answers in the data they needed but with only a third of the metrics to provide.
Say No. If you are in a leadership position, say no, especially. Do not just talk about saying no and respecting the mental well-being of your team. Live it.
Much like a computer, our human brain cannot handle multi-taking the way we think it can. Too many things will crash and burn you.
I self-managed preemptively by taking the time to rest. I knew January would be tough, so I built my reserves ahead of time and communicated openly with my peers and boss about it.
His brilliance in technical ability did not save him. He got written up, which was harmful to his career.
